beats.text: Your CTO asks: "We have 340 branches on the server. Which ones can be deleted without losing anything?"
beats.tele: Your CTO asks: "We have 340 branches on the server. Which ones can be deleted without losing anything?"

beats.text: To answer, you have to know what would be deleted. If a branch is a copy of the code, deleting one deletes code. If a branch is the set of commits that branched off, deleting one deletes commits. A commit, remember, is one saved snapshot of the project. So which is it: a copy, a set of commits, or something else? Say your answer.
beats.tele: To answer, you have to know what would be deleted. If a branch is a copy of the code, deleting one deletes code. If a branch is the set of commits that branched off, deleting one deletes commits. A commit, remember, is one saved snapshot of the project. So which is it: a copy, a set of commits, or something else? Say your answer.

beats.text: Something else. The polls in the course's research report found that 58 percent of practising developers think of a branch as the commits that branched off, and 15 percent as a pointer. The second group is right, in a way that decides outcomes. A branch is one line of text: a name and the ID of one commit. Everything in the next five videos follows from that fact. And the 340 branches? We come back to them before the end.
beats.tele: Something else. The polls in the course's research report found that 58 percent of practising developers think of a branch as the commits that branched off, and 15 percent as a pointer. The second group is right, in a way that decides outcomes. A branch is one line of text: a name and the ID of one commit. Everything in the next five videos follows from that fact. And the 340 branches? We come back to them before the end.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This block of five videos is about refs: branches, HEAD, tags, and the relations between them. A ref is a name for an object ID. The textbook opens the chapter with three CTO questions: the 340 branches, a contractor whose two days of work vanished after she checked out a tag, and every laptop failing with cannot lock ref since this morning. All three are questions about refs, and none has a Git command as its answer.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This block of five videos is about refs: branches, HEAD, tags, and the relations between them. A ref is a name for an object ID. The textbook opens the chapter with three CTO questions: the 340 branches, a contractor whose two days of work vanished after she checked out a tag, and every laptop failing with `cannot lock ref` since this morning. All three are questions about refs, and none has a Git command as its answer.

beats.text: Today we establish the three facts under all of it. A branch is a ref. HEAD is a symbolic ref. And a commit writes one ref: the one that HEAD names.

beats.text: A branch is a ref. In one sentence: a branch is a ref, a name under refs/heads/ that holds the ID of one commit, the tip. The branch's history is whatever that commit reaches through its parents.
beats.tele: A branch is a ref. In one sentence: a branch is a ref, a name under `refs/heads/` that holds the ID of one commit, the tip. The branch's history is whatever that commit reaches through its parents.

beats.text: Precisely, from the glossary: a branch head is "a named reference to the commit at the tip of a branch", stored "in a file in $GIT_DIR/refs/heads/ directory, except when using packed refs". The ref holds nothing but the ID. There's no list of the branch's commits, no record of where it started, no owner, no creation date. git log feature is a walk that starts at the ID in the ref and follows parent lines.
beats.tele: Precisely, from the glossary: a branch head is "a named reference to the commit at the tip of a branch", stored "in a file in $GIT_DIR/refs/heads/ directory, except when using packed refs". The ref holds nothing but the ID. There's no list of the branch's commits, no record of where it started, no owner, no creation date. `git log feature` is a walk that starts at the ID in the ref and follows `parent` lines.

beats.text: Inside .git. With the files backend, which Git 2.55 uses by default, a loose branch is the file .git/refs/heads/<name>, containing the ID and a newline. Packed refs move the same information into lines of .git/packed-refs. The reftable backend keeps refs in a binary store. The reflog of a branch, the journal of where it has pointed, lives in .git/logs/refs/heads/<name>.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`. With the files backend, which Git 2.55 uses by default, a loose branch is the file `.git/refs/heads/<name>`, containing the ID and a newline. Packed refs move the same information into lines of `.git/packed-refs`. The reftable backend keeps refs in a binary store. The reflog of a branch, the journal of where it has pointed, lives in `.git/logs/refs/heads/<name>`.

beats.text: That's why plumbing is the reliable reader. Plumbing means Git's low-level commands, made for scripts, and porcelain means the everyday ones. A script that reads .git/refs/heads/main breaks on the first packed repository, and on every reftable repository.
beats.tele: That's why plumbing is the reliable reader. Plumbing means Git's low-level commands, made for scripts, and porcelain means the everyday ones. A script that reads `.git/refs/heads/main` breaks on the first packed repository, and on every reftable repository.

beats.text: Creating a branch by plumbing. git update-ref writes a ref. It is 🟡 CAUTION. It makes two checks that porcelain also relies on: the object must exist, and a ref under refs/heads/ must name a commit. Writing the file by hand bypasses both checks, the locking and the reflog. The textbook labels hand-written ref files 🔴 DANGEROUS.
beats.tele: Creating a branch by plumbing. `git update-ref` writes a ref. It is 🟡 CAUTION. It makes two checks that porcelain also relies on: the object must exist, and a ref under `refs/heads/` must name a commit. Writing the file by hand bypasses both checks, the locking and the reflog. The textbook labels hand-written ref files 🔴 DANGEROUS.

beats.text: git update-ref -d deletes a ref together with its reflog, with no merge check, and is 🔴 DANGEROUS. What it can destroy is the only name of those commits. The preview is git rev-parse on the ref, writing the ID down. The recovery is to recreate the ref from that ID. And it's appropriate for refs you created yourself, as in today's demo. Twig looks worried, and with a red label on screen, fairly so.
beats.tele: `git update-ref -d` deletes a ref together with its reflog, with no merge check, and is 🔴 DANGEROUS. What it can destroy is the only name of those commits. The preview is `git rev-parse` on the ref, writing the ID down. The recovery is to recreate the ref from that ID. And it's appropriate for refs you created yourself, as in today's demo. Twig looks worried, and with a red label on screen, fairly so.

beats.text: HEAD is a symbolic ref. In one sentence: HEAD is the ref that says where you are: normally a symbolic ref that names the current branch, and in detached state a direct reference to a commit.
beats.tele: HEAD is a symbolic ref. In one sentence: HEAD is the ref that says where you are: normally a symbolic ref that names the current branch, and in detached state a direct reference to a commit.

beats.text: A symbolic ref is, in the manual's words, "a regular file that stores a string that begins with ref: refs/". When HEAD contains ref: refs/heads/main, every command that needs "the current commit" resolves HEAD to refs/heads/main, and then to the ID in that ref. HEAD is per worktree, so each working directory of a repository has its own.
beats.tele: A symbolic ref is, in the manual's words, "a regular file that stores a string that begins with ref: refs/". When HEAD contains `ref: refs/heads/main`, every command that needs "the current commit" resolves HEAD to `refs/heads/main`, and then to the ID in that ref. HEAD is per worktree, so each working directory of a repository has its own.

beats.text: So .git/HEAD has three possible contents. On a branch: the name of a ref that exists. Detached: a commit ID. Unborn: the name of a ref that doesn't exist yet, as in a new repository before the first commit.
beats.tele: So `.git/HEAD` has three possible contents. On a branch: the name of a ref that exists. Detached: a commit ID. Unborn: the name of a ref that doesn't exist yet, as in a new repository before the first commit.

beats.text: What a commit does. In one sentence: a commit writes the new commit's ID into the ref that HEAD names, and nothing else moves. .git/HEAD keeps its text. Other branches stay where they are. Two reflogs gain a line each: the branch's and HEAD's. Those are the two ref writes to trace.
beats.tele: What a commit does. In one sentence: a commit writes the new commit's ID into the ref that HEAD names, and nothing else moves. `.git/HEAD` keeps its text. Other branches stay where they are. Two reflogs gain a line each: the branch's and HEAD's. Those are the two ref writes to trace.

beats.text: When this matters. Because a branch is a name for a commit, "the branch" has a different value in every repository that holds a copy of it: your clone, each colleague's clone, the server. Watch: a teammate pushes a commit, and the server's main moves while yours stays put. main on the server and main in your clone are two refs that happen to share a name. A statement such as "the fix is on main" is only meaningful with a repository attached.
beats.tele: When this matters. Because a branch is a name for a commit, "the branch" has a different value in every repository that holds a copy of it: your clone, each colleague's clone, the server. Watch: a teammate pushes a commit, and the server's `main` moves while yours stays put. `main` on the server and `main` in your clone are two refs that happen to share a name. A statement such as "the fix is on `main`" is only meaningful with a repository attached.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: a branch is a bookmark in a book that is still being written. The bookmark marks one page. The chapters before that page are "the story so far", but they're the book's pages, not the bookmark's. Moving the bookmark changes nothing in the book, and two bookmarks can sit on the same page.
beats.tele: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: a branch is a bookmark in a book that is still being written. The bookmark marks one page. The chapters before that page are "the story so far", but they're the book's pages, not the bookmark's. Moving the bookmark changes nothing in the book, and two bookmarks can sit on the same page.

beats.text: The analogy breaks at the edge: pages after a bookmark exist too, unless nothing points at them, and then Git may eventually throw them away.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks at the edge: pages after a bookmark exist too, unless nothing points at them, and then Git may eventually throw them away.

beats.text: Add HEAD to the picture: a slip of paper on your desk that names the bookmark you're using. When you write a new page, you move that bookmark forward. The slip on the desk still says the same thing.

No Git command wrote this ref, so nothing logged it. git update-ref -d 🔴 DANGEROUS deletes it. The five questions were answered a moment ago, and this ref is one the script created itself.

beats.text: Four ways to read HEAD, from raw to friendly.
beats.tele: Four ways to read HEAD, from raw to friendly.

beats.text: A new repository: HEAD points at refs/heads/main, but no such ref exists until the first commit writes it. git rev-parse --verify HEAD fails, git branch lists nothing, and git branch feature fails, because there's no commit to point the new branch at.
beats.tele: A new repository: HEAD points at `refs/heads/main`, but no such ref exists until the first commit writes it. `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` fails, `git branch` lists nothing, and `git branch feature` fails, because there's no commit to point the new branch at.

beats.text: Now move HEAD alone, with git symbolic-ref HEAD <ref> 🟡 CAUTION. It rewrites one file. Predict what git status reports.
beats.tele: Now move HEAD alone, with `git symbolic-ref HEAD <ref>` 🟡 CAUTION. It rewrites one file. Predict what `git status` reports.

beats.text: The index and the working tree still hold the content of main, so git status reports the difference between the commit HEAD now names and the index as a staged deletion. The index is the list of what goes into the next commit, and the working tree is your files on disk. Switching back makes the report disappear. A branch switch is this ref change plus an update of the index and the working tree. That's the next video.

The index is the list of what goes into the next commit, and the working tree is your files on disk. Switching back makes the report disappear. A branch switch is this ref change plus an update of the index and the working tree. That's the next video.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Describing a branch as a copy or as a set of commits. Root cause: the ref holds one commit ID and nothing else; the history is reached through parent links.
beats.tele: Describing a branch as a copy or as a set of commits. Root cause: the ref holds one commit ID and nothing else; the history is reached through parent links.

beats.text: Reading .git/refs/heads/<name> in a script. Root cause: refs may be packed or stored in reftable; use git rev-parse or git for-each-ref.
beats.tele: Reading `.git/refs/heads/<name>` in a script. Root cause: refs may be packed or stored in reftable; use `git rev-parse` or `git for-each-ref`.

beats.text: Writing a ref file by hand. Root cause: it skips validation, locking and the reflog; use git update-ref.
beats.tele: Writing a ref file by hand. Root cause: it skips validation, locking and the reflog; use `git update-ref`.

beats.text: git branch feature fails in a new repository. Root cause: the current branch is unborn, so there is no commit to point the new branch at.
beats.tele: `git branch feature` fails in a new repository. Root cause: the current branch is unborn, so there is no commit to point the new branch at.

beats.text: Saying "the fix is on main" without naming a repository. Root cause: main is a different ref with possibly a different value in every clone and on the server.
beats.tele: Saying "the fix is on `main`" without naming a repository. Root cause: `main` is a different ref with possibly a different value in every clone and on the server.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. "I committed to the wrong branch" is, as the textbook puts it, a ref problem and not a content problem. The commit object is correct. Only the name that moved is wrong. An engineer on an evaluation team makes two commits on main that belong on a feature branch. Nothing has to be copied. The repair is two ref writes: create a branch at the current commit, and move main back. Video 26 runs that repair.

beats.text: And the CTO's 340 branches? Deleting a branch deletes a name. Whether anything is lost depends on whether another name still reaches those commits. That's a reachability question, and video 26 answers it with three tests.
